L.A. City Council Passes New Motions Aimed at Film-Friendly Overhaul
articles.content: As filming levels in the city continue their downward momentum, the Los Angeles City Council passed two measures in a meeting on Wednesday to attempt to stem the bleeding. The measures, both introduced by City Councilmember Adrin Nazarian, create a free microshoot permit for ultra-small productions and open up city-owned parking lots, yards, civic properties and staging areas to productions for just $1 a day. The microshoot motion will provide small projects with 10 or fewer production personnel with permits to film on-location in L.A. without a fee, making filmmaking less onerous and expensive for student filmmakers, documentary crews and ultra-low-budget projects in the city. As for the second motion, the idea is to make city-owned spaces that films and television shows generally use for base camp, crew parking and other low-impact activities more accessible and affordable. “Today marks a major milestone for the Keep Hollywood Home campaign,” Nazarian said in a statement. “With these latest actions, all Phase 1 motions have now been approved by the City. This progress demonstrates the impact of the Ad Hoc Committee and our commitment to keep up the pressure for real reforms.” The development arrives less than a week after city film office FilmLA found that shoot days for film and television in the city continued to fall from June to September in spite of local and state efforts to encourage more production to return to the city. L.A.’s shoot days dropped nearly five percent compared to the same period in 2025 and 11 percent from the previous quarter. In 2025, California more than doubled the funding available for its film and television tax credit program, from a previous $330 million a year to $750 million. On a more local level, Mayor Karen Bass issued an executive order in 2025 to streamline the city’s permitting process. Meanwhile, seven initial motions from Nazarian to improve filming practices in L.A. passed the full Council earlier this year .

articles.content: Opposition is mounting among some major Hollywood studios against the California Film Commission’s diversity initiative designed to encourage more inclusive hiring on movies and TV series. At the heart of their frustration: concerns that compliance could violate federal law as the government cracks down on diversity programs hailed not too long ago as representing a much-needed step forward in getting films and TV shows to more accurately reflect audiences in California and the rest of the world. In recent years, Disney, Amazon Studios and Skydance, among others, have quietly retreated from diversity efforts, like tying staffing goals to race, ethnicity and gender. Participation in the state’s diversity initiative, which gives movies and TV shows a small bump in their overall tax credit, isn’t mandatory. Productions, however, risk leaving money on the table by choosing not to opt in. Over the course of multiple films, it can net studios a hefty sum. For California, criticism of the program has emerged as yet another roadblock to restoring production in the state amid a global tit-for-tat battle to host Hollywood. The pushback to the initiative climaxed in June at a commission meeting, reviewed by The Hollywood Reporter , in which board members employed by the studios and unions expressed significant reservations about whether it should move forward as currently constructed because of legal and administrative issues. Arturo Barquet, a board member and CFO of Global Production Operations for Universal Filmed Entertainment, said that Universal has “many times considered whether we should opt out.” “There are regulations — there are things in here that are in conflict with federal law,” he added. After the birth of the star system in Hollywood, Parsons and Hopper rose to prominence as gossip columnists who could make and break careers, and choose to keep or expose celebrities’ secrets. With a combined readership of 75 million at their peak, Hopper and Parsons wielded extraordinary influence — and instilled paralyzing fear. Kramer was speaking at an Academy in Tokyo panel at the Tokyo International Film Festival alongside Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor and chief membership, impact and industry officer Meredith Shea, moderated by festival director Hisamatsu Takeo. articles.content: The Oscars will keep honoring human-driven work as AI spreads through filmmaking, Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor tells Variety in Tokyo, while the Academy’s leadership expects to keep refining the international feature rules in the first year of a new route that lets festivals qualify films. Howell Taylor, Academy CEO Bill Kramer , chief membership, impact and industry officer Meredith Shea and Amy Homma, director and president of the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and Academy Collection, are in Japan for the Tokyo International Film Festival to meet members and filmmakers. articles.content: The opening film of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival , Zeze Takahisa ’s “ Sukiyaki ” tells the story of how the title tune became a worldwide hit in 1963 as well as a beloved standard that has been recorded in foreign-language versions that have also topped charts. The film goes beyond the song itself to delve into the lives and careers of its makers: lyricist Ei Roksuke (Matsuzaka Tori), composer Nakamura Hachidai (Okada Junichi), and singer Sakamoto Kyu (Nakano Taiga). They became known in Japan as the “689 trio” with the unusual moniker coming from the “number” characters in their names: Hachi (8), Roku (6) and Kyu (9). But as the film shows in scene after highly charged dramatic scene, their professional and personal relationships were not always harmonious. articles.title: Horror Film ‘The Land of Jinn’ Is First Indonesia-Kyrgyzstan Co-Production, Unveiled at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
articles.content: Indonesia and Kyrgyzstan have made their first film together. “The Land of Jinn ,” a supernatural horror feature directed by Kevin Rahardjo (“Smothered”), was unveiled at the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market as the first co-production between the two countries. The story centers on a young Indonesian woman who journeys to Kyrgyzstan in search of a mystical healer who might save the baby she is carrying. articles.content: A Himalayan drama that sets a grandmother’s stories against the rise of artificial intelligence is aiming for a Cannes premiere next year. Director Bikash Subedi’s Nepali feature “ Shirjara : Song of Grandmother” has wrapped principal photography and is at the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market to raise its last $44,000. Described as a speculative drama, the film moves between the traditional culture of the high Himalayas and a modern world shaped by technology. Its central question is what people building learning machines might gain from the knowledge of their ancestors – knowledge kept alive outside written archives and digital databases. articles.title: ‘60 Minutes’ Audience Sinks to Surprising Low Without Football
articles.content: It’s not surprising to see ratings at “ 60 Minutes ” slump when CBS doesn’t air a strong football game before the start of the show. The fifth episode of this season’s cycle of the venerable CBS newsmagazine drew only 5.64 million viewers, one of the smallest audiences for the program in years, according to data from Nielsen. The show captured a mere 558,000 among viewers between 25 and 54, the demographic coveted most by advertisers in news programming. articles.title: Academy CEO Bill Kramer Makes the Case for a More Global Oscars at Tokyo Film Festival
articles.summary: Kramer says international membership growth, the Oscars-YouTube deal, and a new festival-qualifying pathway to nomination are all part of the organization’s expanding worldwide ambitions.
articles.content: The U.S. may be growing ever more isolationist under the “America First” rubric of President Donald Trump, but the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences remains steadfastly global in its outlook and ambitions. That was the thrust of Academy CEO Bill Kramer ’s comments at the Tokyo International Film Festival on Wednesday, where he spoke at length about his organization’s ongoing efforts to bring more international filmmakers and film lovers into the Oscars fold. “The Academy is becoming more and more global across programs, and as part of that, you’re seeing a great increase in the number of academy members who live outside of the United States,” Kramer said. He noted the oft-cited fact that a decade ago just 5 percent of Academy members were based outside the U.S., compared with 25 percent today. And in a hat tip to the local crowd, Kramer said the Academy has about 70 Japanese members, but that he expects that number to climb. Related Stories Movies Tokyo: 'All of A Sudden' Star Tao Okamoto Honored With The Hollywood Reporter's Trailblazer Award Movies Meet the Estonian Folklore Characters Helping to Celebrate the 30th Tallinn Fest - and Their Animator “This is all part of our drive to create a more diverse and inclusive academy,” he said. Kramer also underscored that Oscars nominations have already begun to reflect the increasingly cosmopolitan tastes of the member base. “At the last Oscars, every category had international representation. It’s not just found in the international feature film category — this trend includes our best picture category,” he explained. “Of course, everybody remembers the moment when Parasite won best picture. That was sort of a pivot, or a shift, I think, in our thinking about what was possible with global cinema at the Oscars, and that continues.” Kramer asserted that the Academy’s somewhat controversial deal with YouTube was inspired by this same desire to cultivate deeper ties with filmmakers and film lovers across the globe.

articles.title: Tokyo Film Festival Director Takeo Hisamatsu Wants More Money, More Parties and a Bigger Global Profile for Japanese Cinema
articles.summary: Returning to lead the festival ahead of its 40th anniversary, the industry veteran sees an opportunity to capitalize on the surging international interest in all things Japan.

Ando made a spate of swift changes, relocating the festival to Tokyo’s glitzy Ginza and Hibiya districts, shaking up its programming staff, adding more filmmaker talks and reviving the Kurosawa Akira Award. articles.content: Over the past few years you may have noticed a Jewish-themed comic popping up in your social media feed. Now Modi is getting the next feather in his media cap: a documentary. Filmmakers Seth Kramer and Daniel A. Miller, Emmy nominees who have specialized in outsider performers and their effect on an in-audience, are directing the movie, with The Big Bang Theory star Mayim Bialik (and self-confessed Modi superfan) serving as both onscreen commentator and executive producer. articles.title: ‘VisionQuest’: Who Is Raza, the Surprise Bad Guy in Episode 6?
articles.summary: You've definitely seen him before The post ‘VisionQuest’: Who Is Raza, the Surprise Bad Guy in Episode 6? appeared first on TheWrap .
articles.content: We’re nearing the end of “VisionQuest,” with Episodes 5 and 6 now streaming on Disney+. With them came a new face in the story, as the hunt for Vision continued — but he’s not actually all that new. In Episode 6, we find Vision (Paul Bettany) meeting up with Paladin (Todd Stashwick) to negotiate. Soon enough though, their meeting is interrupted by gunfire, and a whole squad of goons. At the head of them is a bald man, who Paladin immediately knows as Raza. And if you’re thinking he looks familiar to you too, you’re correct. You might remember Raza, played by Faran Tahir, as one of the earliest bad guys introduced in the MCU. He was the leader of the Ten Rings, who held Tony Stark captive in a cave and forced him to build a Jericho missile for the terrorist group. Instead, Tony used the supplies to build his very first Iron Man suit. Yes, this is the same Ten Rings organization as explained in “Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings,” founded by Shang-Chi’s father. When last we saw Raza, he was being temporarily paralyzed by Obadiah Stane (Jeff Bridges) in “Iron Man.” Stane double-crossed Raza after the two worked together to capture Tony Stark, thus revealing Stane’s deception to the audience. This marks his first appearance in the MCU since that 2008 film. Alongside Bettany, that means that Tahir has technically been the longest-employed actor in the MCU, appearing in both the franchise’s first project and its most recent (until “Avengers: Doomsday,” when Robert Downey Jr. will take back that crown). You really don’t need to remember much about Raza or his arc in “Iron Man,” because he is not actually the mystery client who hired Paladin. Rather, he’s an extra set of hands hired by said client to help capture Vision.

On “Donnie Darko” overcoming its box office shortcomings and transforming into a cult classic, Rogen noted, “If a thing is good and resonates, it will find its people. According to the report, Panahi’s lawyer, Mostafa Nili, said Panahi was also issued a two-year travel ban and a two-year prohibition on social media activity. articles.summary: Daniel Lombroso's certainly bizarre but sensitive portrait follows a PhalloFill entrepreneur (it's what it sounds like) and two of his clients as they walk us through a cosmetic phenomenon whose main clientele are insecure men.
articles.content: What if you could up your penis size a notch or two with a few spritzes of a needle? OK, it’s not that simple, but the PhaloFILL procedure highlighted by filmmaker Daniel Lombroso in his latest documentary, “ Manhood ,” aims to make penile enlargement procedures about as easy (and commonplace) as Botox. Dallas entrepreneur Bill Moore, who is quite proudly Botoxed and fillered-up himself, patented the minimally invasive procedure (don’t call it plastic surgery!), promising to make insecure men feel whole again. Or at least a bit thicker, anyway. Lombroso’s skillfully constructed film is funny in the best and worst ways: funny because it’s in on the joke but “funny” because of how the majority of the audience might feel embarrassed just by watching it. The director understands the humor inherent to this situation, but he also understands the sad parts, the well of male insecurity it’s all coming from — locating that especially in an OnlyFans camboy who comes to Moore after a catastrophic procedure at a rival clinic has left him with a dick full of nodules. articles.summary: Nathan Fielder's doc is a cultural sensation, but it's unlikely to match the fervor around Michael Moore's seminal George W. Bush screed.
articles.content: It’s too early to say if Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “ You Can See Everything ” will win Oscars or have a direct impact on history as it pertains to Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos, but it does feel like a movie that journalists are going to be referencing for a long time as a significant benchmark for documentary films at the box office . Currently sitting at $45.1 million domestic , with no international release to speak of yet, A24’s film is already one of the highest-grossing documentaries ever. Domestically (not factoring inflation) it has already placed firmly within the top 10 and has obliterated films like “Free Solo” ($17.5 million), “Won’t You Be My Neighbor” ($22.8 million), and “An Inconvenient Truth” ($24.1 million). articles.summary: Ray Nicholson and Bill Skarsgård star in an unexceptional sports drama that falls well short of a first down.
articles.content: There have been any number of movies about the hell of fighting in World War II , the most visceral of which have been made in the years since “Saving Private Ryan” provided a very enduring template for how modern filmmakers could render that carnage with both the spectacle of a blockbuster and the horror of a memory. Peter Berg’s brutal and concussive “ The Mosquito Bowl ” is definitely one of them! No one could ever say that it’s not. What differentiates this unsparing epic from the scores of other stories about the Greatest Generation, however, is that some of its characters are good at football. Indeed, these All-American college boys are so good at football that, on Christmas Eve 1944, the soldiers are ordered to play a morale-boosting game of two-hand touch on the beach where their units are preparing for the Battle of Okinawa. articles.content: Early in “The Gilded Age” Season 4, during a moment of great tension, a hoity-toity British doctor in a cravat loses his senses and snaps at Bertha Russell ( Carrie Coon ): “Let me be clear,” the doctor hisses. “You do not understand the situation. Please leave me .” Bertha, with little more than a flick of her bulging eyes (which could mean anything from “Oh shit” to “If this goes wrong, I will roast your heart over the raging pyre of your dismembered corpse”), does as she’s urged and retreats. The precarious circumstances don’t allow for pushback — time is of the essence — and Bertha, in her boundless wisdom, knows she has no choice but to trust this man and his alleged expertise. articles.title: Luchino Visconti’s Tragic, Beautiful Final Film ‘L’Innocente’ Restored in 4K — Watch the Trailer
articles.summary: The 1976 marital melodrama joins Visconti classics like "White Nights" and "Conversation Piece" in returning to theaters, restored.
articles.content: Luchino Visconti ‘s lush, aristocratic worlds have seen a major revival at repertory movie houses over the past year. From the black-and-white “ White Nights ” with Marcello Mastroianni to the psychosexual queer drama “Conversation Piece” with Burt Lancaster, the Italian grandmaster’s vivid melodramas capture souls adrift, possessive , and tragic. While Visconti is probably best known for epics like “The Leopard” and “Rocco and His Brothers,” in his later career up until his death in 1976, the Palme d’Or-winning filmmaker turned his lens on more intimate dramas and marital discord. A new restoration of Visconti’s final film , “L’Innocente,” premiered in Cannes Classics and at the New York Film Festival . Starring Giancarlo Giannini, Laura Antonelli, and Jennifer O’Neill, the film was lovingly restored by Film Movement Classics to preserve the film’s 50th anniversary. Below, IndieWire debuts the exclusive trailer for the new release. A theatrical rollout begins December 11. Wounded by his years of neglect, Giuliana takes a lover of her own with young novelist, Filippo (Marc Porel).
